uncited: This family implements optical effects that deviate from the ideal pinhole camera model, primarily depth of field (blur based on focal distance) and geometric lens distortions.

It sets itself apart from sibling ray generation methods by introducing a finite aperture for ray origins, requiring sampling over a 2D area rather than a single point, and by modifying ray directions to simulate optical phenomena like magnification or shift.
The core mechanism shared by all methods in this family is the modification of the ray origin $\mathbf{o}$ and/or direction $\mathbf{d}$ based on a sampled point on a lens aperture.
Unlike the pinhole model where $\mathbf{o}$ is fixed at the camera eye, here $\mathbf{o}$ is displaced onto a lens plane defined by a center, normal, and radius.
The direction $\mathbf{d}$ is often recalculated to pass through a specific focus point or to maintain geometric consistency with the new origin.
Rays originate from points sampled on a 2D disk (or other shape) representing the lens aperture.
The sampling distribution (e.g., uniform, concentric) determines the shape of the bokeh (blur circles) in the final image.
The probability density function (PDF) of the sampling must be accounted for in path tracing integrals via importance weighting.
For depth of field, the ray direction is typically computed as the vector from the sampled lens point to a target focus point in the scene.
For lens shift or distortion, the direction may be rotated or scaled relative to the optical axis.

When transforming samples between different aperture geometries or sizes (e.g., in multi-view rendering), the Jacobian determinant of the transformation must be computed to preserve the correct probability density for Monte Carlo integration.
A procedural approach to generating DOF rays using noise buffers and distance-based offsets.
It generates an offset using a noise buffer and lens distance, transforms it to world space, and calculates the new ray direction and origin based on the distance to focus.
It performs AABB intersection on the resulting rays.
This method is distinct from analytical thin lens sampling by relying on noise-driven perturbations rather than uniform disk sampling.
Lens shift techniques for multi-view rendering address the specific problem of sample reuse in volumetric contexts where aperture sizes vary.
